item.title: Who Gets to Define Beauty?
item.description:
Body Image

Who Gets to Define Beauty?

What makes appearance compliments so complicated.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Beauty standards shape not only how we see ourselves but also how we hear compliments.
  • Appearance compliments can reflect genuine appreciation or reinforce narrow cultural ideals.
  • Beauty is richer than cultural standards and includes presence, connection, and individuality.

Someone says, "You look beautiful today."

Instead of feeling good, your mind immediately responds:

They're just being nice.

They don't really mean it.

I don't know what they're seeing.

For many people, receiving a compliment about their appearance is surprisingly uncomfortable. Rather than taking it in, they question it, dismiss it, or explain it away. Why can something intended as kindness be so difficult to believe? The answer often lies in the intersection of our personal experiences and the messages we've learned about beauty.

Why Appearance Compliments Can Feel So Complicated

Source: Annie Spratt/Unsplash

One of the things I notice repeatedly as a psychotherapist is that people routinely struggle to accept compliments that conflict with the story they already believe about themselves. If someone has come to believe they are unattractive, hearing "you look great" doesn't feel reassuring. It feels inaccurate. When our internal narrative and someone else's observation don't match, many of us are quicker to question the compliment than our own self-perception.

When we've spent years believing we are unattractive, inadequate, or "not enough," criticism often feels believable while compliments feel suspect. A single negative comment about appearance can stay with someone for years, even a lifetime, while dozens of genuine compliments fade almost instantly.

Body image is not simply how we look. It is how we experience living in our bodies. Two people can receive the very same compliment and have completely different reactions. One person may appreciate the compliment without feeling defined by it, while another immediately wonders whether the compliment means they looked better than they did yesterday, whether they're expected to maintain that appearance, or whether their value is being reduced to how they look.

Our personal histories shape the lens through which we hear compliments. Experiences such as bullying, weight stigma, trauma, and perfectionism can all influence how we interpret what others say. At the same time, not all appearance compliments communicate the same message. Some reflect one person's genuine appreciation of another's individuality. Others reinforce narrow cultural ideals by privileging thinness, youthfulness, and certain facial features.

Sometimes our discomfort comes from the beliefs we've internalized about ourselves. Sometimes it comes from the messages embedded in the compliment itself. More often, it's a combination of both. Neither our personal filters nor the compliments we exchange develop in isolation. Both are shaped by the culture around us.

Who Gets to Define Beauty?

Long before most of us begin questioning our appearance, we've already absorbed countless messages about what beauty is supposed to look like. Western beauty ideals have long elevated thinness, youth, light skin, certain facial features, and particular body shapes, treating them as objective truths rather than cultural ideals. Repeated exposure can make them feel natural, inevitable, and universal. We stop experiencing them as socially constructed and begin treating them as facts.

When we don't see ourselves reflected in those ideals, it can become difficult to believe that someone genuinely finds us beautiful. We assume they're just being polite, exaggerating, or they’re just not noticing our flaws. In those moments, we may place more trust in cultural beauty standards than in another person's genuine experience of us. That raises a larger question: Who gets to decide what beauty is?

Expanding Our Definition of Beauty

If beauty standards are socially constructed rather than universal truths, then our definition of beauty may be far narrower than it needs to be. Some appearance compliments reinforce that narrow definition. Comments such as "you've lost weight" or "you look so young" often equate thinness and youth with beauty, success, and worth. Even when they're intended kindly, they imply that looking smaller or younger is inherently more desirable. We also rarely know why someone's body has changed. Weight loss may reflect grief, illness, stress, depression, medication, or an eating disorder rather than improved health or happiness. Similarly, complimenting someone for looking younger can unintentionally reinforce the idea that aging is something to resist rather than a natural part of being human.

Looking beyond those messages doesn't mean avoiding appearance altogether. It means recognizing that beauty is much broader than the standards we've inherited. It can be found in expressive eyes, freckles, silver hair, laugh lines that reflect years of joy, or hands that show a lifetime of creating, caring, or working. It can be found in someone's warmth, laugh, quiet confidence, or ability to make others feel seen and valued. It can also be found in features that connect someone to their family, heritage, culture, or personal history.

Source: George Dagerotip/Unsplash

I've come to see my own nose differently. It's beautiful to me not because it fits any conventional beauty ideal but because it reminds me of my father and my grandfather. For someone else, beauty might be found in freckles that reflect their heritage, hair that connects them to their culture, or a feature that reminds them of someone important in their life. Those qualities matter not because they meet a cultural ideal but because they tell a story about identity, connection, and belonging.

Looking at Beauty Differently

Healing from a painful relationship with your body and appearance isn't about believing every compliment you receive, nor is it about depending on compliments to determine your worth. It begins with questioning the standards you've been using to evaluate yourself and others. If those standards are narrow, socially constructed, and constantly reinforced, they don't deserve the authority we've given them.

When we begin to broaden our definition of beauty, appearance compliments no longer have to compete with an impossible ideal. Instead, they become opportunities to recognize something genuine and meaningful in another person and, sometimes, in ourselves.
